intro: No one reads the Analects or the Daodejing alone. Every reader stands in a long line of earlier readers. Some wrote notes between the lines. Some made the classics into exam answers. Some attacked them in the streets. Some carried them to new countries and new languages.

In this unit you meet those readers. First come the great commentators: He Yan and Wang Bi in the third century, Zhu Xi in the twelfth and Wang Yangming in the fifteenth and sixteenth. Then come modern readers: May Fourth critics, Cultural Revolution campaigns, New Confucian revivalists, feminist scholars, Confucius Institutes, and Western readers from the Jesuits to Ursula K. Le Guin.

By the end you will be able to explain how a commentary shapes a classic, compare two readings of the same line, describe why the classics have been attacked and revived, and write a short reception history that attributes every view and ranks none.
bigQuestion: Who decides what a classic means, and how do readers across centuries change the texts they read?

test.q: Why is commentary called the main genre of Chinese philosophy?
choices: Many thinkers built new ideas by explaining classics
Commentary was the only legal writing
No one wrote treatises in any culture
test.why: Thinkers like Wang Bi and Zhu Xi did philosophy through commentary.

test.q: What did Wang Bi stress in the Daodejing?
choices: Nonbeing as the root of all things
test.why: Wang Bi's commentary centers on wu.

test.q: Which two terms are central to Zhu Xi's account of the world?
test.why: For Zhu Xi, all things have principle and qi.

test.q: How did Zhu Xi read gewu?
test.why: Zhu Xi read it outward, as investigating things.

test.q: Who tried to investigate the principle of bamboo and fell ill?
test.why: Wang Yangming tells the bamboo story.

test.q: What did Wang Yangming teach about knowing and acting?
test.why: He taught the unity of knowledge and action.

test.q: In which year did Zhu Xi's readings become the exam standard?
test.why: The Yuan dynasty adopted them in 1313.

test.q: What was the May Fourth Movement's main complaint about Confucian tradition?
choices: It kept women, the young and the poor in their places
test.why: May Fourth writers linked the old order to many social harms.

choices: Red Guards damaged the Confucius temple and cemetery
test.why: The Cultural Revolution attacked the Qufu sites.

test.q: What did the 1958 New Confucian manifesto argue?
choices: Confucian culture has a living core open to democracy and science
test.why: The manifesto defended a living core open to modern ideas.

test.q: Which Korean scholar is a leading follower of Zhu Xi?
test.why: Toegye was a leading Joseon scholar of Zhu Xi's school.

test.q: Which Western reader saw nonviolence in the Daodejing?
test.why: Tolstoy linked it with his own teaching of nonviolence.
Critics raised concerns about academic freedom.

choices: One who belongs to the text's tradition
test.why: Insiders read as members of the tradition.

test.q: Which Daodejing chapter do some feminist readers cite for keeping to the female?
test.why: Chapter 28 advises knowing the male but keeping to the female.

write.prompt: Choose one line read differently by two readers in this unit (for example the Great Learning's gewu in Zhu Xi and Wang Yangming, or the Analects in May Fourth critics and New Confucians). Cite the text, explain each reading and the problem it answered, and explain why they differ.
tips: Name the text and passage, and say whether you quote or paraphrase.
Attribute every view to its reader: "Zhu Xi read," "May Fourth critics argued."
Explain the historical problem each reader faced.
Use terms such as commentary, orthodoxy and reception history.
Compare the readings; do not declare a winner.
